title: Metric Framing Specifications: How to Select Steel Studs, Track, and Spacing
description: Learn how to specify metric steel studs, track, spacing, loads, and accessories without confusing soft conversions with actual product dimensions.
html:
Metric framing specifications should do more than convert inches to millimetres. A usable specification connects the project’s design intent to the correct steel studs, track, spacing, deflection provisions, loads, finishes, quantities, and technical documentation. This matters whether you are preparing drawings, reviewing a submittal, or requesting a quotation.

In Canadian construction, familiar spacing values such as 300, 400, and 600 mm may represent soft conversions of 12, 16, and 24 inches rather than genuinely metric product dimensions. Confirm the design basis and the manufacturer’s available profiles before treating any number as an exact ordering requirement.

Quick summary

  • Identify whether the assembly is non-load-bearing interior framing or load-bearing structural framing.
  • State whether dimensions are nominal, actual, or soft-converted metric values.
  • Specify stud depth, thickness or gauge, spacing, wall height, loads, track type, deflection needs, and accessories.
  • Check manufacturer load tables, product documentation, and the building requirements for the project’s jurisdiction.
  • Send the supplier complete dimensions, quantities, delivery information, and required submittals before ordering.

What “Metric” Means in Steel Framing Specifications

Metric notation and metric manufacturing are not always the same thing. Canadian guidance commonly expresses 12-inch, 16-inch, and 24-inch framing spacing as 300, 400, and 600 mm on centre. These values are often practical conversions of customary spacing, not proof that every associated stud, track, panel, or accessory was manufactured to a fully metric dimension.

Industry Canada guidance gives 400 mm as the metric expression of 16-inch framing spacing and 600 mm as the expression of 24-inch spacing. It also notes that rigid panels should be designed to suit the framing spacing, including a commonly referenced 1200 mm panel width. Review the Canadian guidance on framing spacing and panel coordination when checking how the grid affects the rest of the assembly.

For a project specification, write the value and its meaning clearly. For example, “studs at 400 mm on centre, subject to approved assembly documentation” is more useful than simply writing “400 mm studs.” The first wording identifies spacing. The second could be misread as a product length, flange dimension, or other member measurement.

Common Metric Spacing Expressions: Use Them as a Starting Point

The following comparison is a coordination reference, not a universal design table. The project drawings, wall assembly, panel layout, manufacturer documentation, and applicable code control the final spacing.

Common customary spacingCommon metric expressionSpecification caution
12 inches on centre300 mm on centreConfirm whether the project requires a soft conversion or an actual metric layout.
16 inches on centre400 mm on centreCoordinate with panel widths, openings, fasteners, and the approved assembly.
24 inches on centre600 mm on centreDo not assume this spacing is suitable for every height, load, finish, or performance requirement.

Canadian construction guidance identifies 300, 400, and 600 mm as metric expressions of 12-, 16-, and 24-inch spacing. However, Ontario code provisions also use millimetre values such as 406, 508, and 610 mm for specified applications. That difference illustrates why a converted spacing should not automatically replace the value in the project’s governing design or code reference. Check the applicable Ontario Building Code provisions for the specific application rather than borrowing a general spacing convention.

Choose the Framing System Before Specifying Dimensions

Begin with the function of the wall or framing assembly. Dass Metal Products offers light-gauge, non-load-bearing steel studs as well as heavy-gauge load-bearing stud framing systems. Those categories should not be treated as interchangeable simply because both use steel studs and track.

Light-gauge non-load-bearing framing

Non-load-bearing light gauge steel framing is commonly selected for interior partitions and other assemblies where the studs are not designed to carry building gravity loads. The specification still needs to address wall height, spacing, board or finish type, openings, attachment requirements, acoustic or fire objectives where applicable, and any movement at the head of the wall.

For a broader selection process, see this guide to choosing a cold-formed steel framing system. It can help organize the relationship between member selection, the wall assembly, and project constraints.

Heavy-gauge load-bearing framing

Load-bearing stud framing requires a different level of verification. The design may depend on axial loads, lateral loads, wall height, stud spacing, bracing, connections, openings, and support conditions. A nominal gauge or stud depth alone does not demonstrate that a member is adequate.

Use the design documents and manufacturer load tables to identify a suitable member. Where the framing is structural, the project’s engineer or other qualified design professional must establish or approve the design basis. This load-bearing steel stud checklist covers important information to confirm before specifying or ordering.

The Details Every Metric Framing Specification Should Include

A complete specification gives the supplier enough information to identify the intended product without guessing. Include the following details where they apply:

  • Project and jurisdiction: Identify the site location, province or territory, building type, and the code framework being used.
  • Framing function: State whether the assembly is non-load-bearing, load-bearing, exterior structural, shaftwall, partition, furred wall, or another application.
  • Member identity: Name the stud or profile, including depth, flange dimensions, lip or return details, and thickness or gauge where specified.
  • Metric basis: State whether each dimension is an actual millimetre dimension, a nominal size, or a soft conversion from customary units.
  • Spacing and orientation: Give the on-centre spacing, direction, layout at openings, and any changes at corners or intersections.
  • Wall geometry: Provide wall height, span, support conditions, openings, deflection zones, and unusual transitions.
  • Loads and performance: Identify gravity, lateral, wind, impact, acoustic, fire, thermal, or finish requirements that affect member selection.
  • Track and connections: Specify standard track, deep track, slotted deflection track, clips, fasteners, bridging, carrying channel, or other required components.
  • Finish assembly: Identify gypsum or other boards, panel orientation, layers, insulation, resilient components, and attachment requirements.
  • Quantity and logistics: State member lengths, counts, accessory quantities, packaging needs, delivery location, and required delivery window.
  • Documentation: List the required brochures, load tables, standards, safety data sheets, drawings, certificates, or submittal forms.

If the design calls for a profile that is not clearly represented by a standard product, describe the geometry and application rather than relying on an informal nickname. A separate guide to what to specify for a custom steel profile can help structure that request.

Match the Track and Accessories to the Wall Condition

Track is part of the framing system, not merely a packaging accessory. Standard track may suit a conventional stud-to-track connection, while deep track can provide a different relationship between the track and the stud. Slotted deflection track is intended for conditions where movement at the head of a wall must be addressed through the specified assembly and connection method.

Do not select track based only on a similar-looking width. Confirm that the track accommodates the stud depth and thickness, suits the connection detail, and matches the wall’s movement, height, and loading requirements. If deflection is expected, the specification should identify the required track or clip arrangement and the movement provisions shown in the design.

Other components also depend on the assembly. Bridging channel or carrying channel may be required for support or alignment. Resilient channel may be part of an acoustic wall or ceiling build-up. Clips such as deflection side clips, webslide clips, or bridging clips should be named only when they correspond to the approved detail. Finishing profiles, furring channel, Z-bar, flat strips, and cornerbead likewise need to match the finish and substrate condition.

Use Load Tables and Product Documentation Before Ordering

Manufacturer load tables help compare candidate members against the design assumptions. They are useful for checking factors such as stud size, thickness, spacing, wall height, support conditions, and loading, but they do not replace project-specific structural design or code review.

Dass Metal Products provides technical resources including product brochures, load tables, standards, and MSDS documentation. When requesting a quotation or submittal, ask which document applies to the proposed profile and whether the table uses the same units, spacing basis, support conditions, and loading assumptions as the project.

Review the documents for more than a product name. Confirm the exact profile, material thickness, dimensions, limiting conditions, connection assumptions, and revision status. If the proposed product differs from the drawing or design schedule, record the substitution and obtain the required review before fabrication or installation.

Separate Ontario Code Checks From General Canadian Practice

Building requirements are jurisdiction-specific in Canada. The National Building Code provides a model framework, but provincial and territorial governments may adopt it with modifications or enact their own requirements. The Government of Canada notes that these authorities regulate building design and construction within their jurisdictions. Confirm the applicable national and provincial code framework before relying on a general Canadian reference.

For an Ontario project, review the applicable Ontario provisions, referenced standards, approved assemblies, and project-specific design documents. An Ontario spacing or support value should not automatically be applied to a project in Alberta, British Columbia, Quebec, or another jurisdiction. The same caution applies when a project crosses provincial or national borders.

How to Prepare a Complete Supplier Request

A supplier request should turn the drawing and design intent into an unambiguous purchasing brief. Use this sequence:

  1. Identify the project: Give the site location, jurisdiction, application, delivery point, and project contact.
  2. Describe the assembly: State the wall or framing function, wall height, finish layers, openings, and whether it is interior, exterior, shaftwall, or structural.
  3. Define the members: List stud profile, depth, thickness or gauge, actual metric dimensions, spacing, lengths, and any required end conditions.
  4. Define the track and accessories: Identify standard, deep, or slotted deflection track, clips, bridging channel, resilient channel, fasteners, trims, and other components.
  5. State the design checks: Provide loads, deflection requirements, limiting-height information, performance requirements, and the professional or approved document governing selection.
  6. List quantities and submittals: Include counts, cut lengths, waste assumptions, delivery needs, load tables, product data, standards, and safety documentation.

Write “400 mm on centre, soft conversion of 16 inches” if that is the design basis. If the drawing instead requires an actual 400 mm layout or a different millimetre value, say so explicitly. Resolve this distinction before quotation, fabrication, or field layout.

Common Metric Framing Specification Mistakes

  • Assuming 300, 400, or 600 mm is correct for every wall assembly.
  • Confusing stud depth or length with stud spacing.
  • Ordering a stud without confirming compatible track dimensions.
  • Using nominal gauge as a substitute for a complete member specification.
  • Omitting wall height, loads, openings, bracing, or head-of-wall movement.
  • Specifying spacing without identifying the board or finish assembly.
  • Applying Ontario guidance to another jurisdiction without verification.
  • Requesting a quotation without quantities, delivery location, or required documentation.

A Four-Step Decision Path Before You Order

  1. Identify the assembly. Decide whether the framing is non-load-bearing, load-bearing, exterior, shaftwall, acoustic, or a finishing support system.
  2. Verify design and code requirements. Confirm spacing, loads, height, deflection, performance requirements, and the governing jurisdiction.
  3. Confirm members and documentation. Match studs, track, clips, bridging, finishes, and accessories to the approved details and applicable load tables.
  4. Submit a complete request. Give the supplier metric dimensions, conversion assumptions, quantities, delivery information, and submittal requirements.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are 300 mm, 400 mm, and 600 mm steel stud spacings true metric dimensions?

They are commonly used metric expressions of 12-, 16-, and 24-inch on-centre spacing. They may therefore be soft conversions rather than evidence that every related product dimension is metric. Confirm the project’s design basis and the manufacturer’s product information.

Can I use the same metric framing specification across Canadian provinces?

No. General Canadian practice can help with terminology and coordination, but building requirements are jurisdiction-specific. Confirm the code, referenced standards, approved assemblies, and design requirements for the province or territory where the work will occur.

What is the difference between light-gauge non-load-bearing studs and heavy-gauge load-bearing framing?

Light-gauge non-load-bearing studs are selected for assemblies where the studs are not designed to carry building gravity loads. Heavy-gauge load-bearing framing is selected and verified for structural demands such as axial or lateral loading, support conditions, wall height, bracing, and connections. The correct choice requires project-specific design information.

Which documents should I request with a metric steel framing quotation?

Request product data for the proposed profiles, applicable load tables, installation or assembly details, relevant standards or certifications, and safety data documentation where required. Also identify any drawings, substitutions, or submittal forms needed for project approval.

Conclusion: Verify the Assembly Before You Specify the Material

A strong metric framing specification does not stop at a millimetre spacing value. It identifies the framing function, distinguishes soft conversions from actual dimensions, matches studs with track and accessories, states the design conditions, and points to the documents used for verification.

Before ordering, identify the assembly, confirm the applicable jurisdiction and design requirements, review the relevant load tables and product information, and send the supplier a complete request.
